solutions.body:
The equation is $\min(2x,\,x+2,\,1)=\min(x,2)$.

- If $x<\frac12$: $2x<1$ and $2x<x+2$, so the left side is $2x$, and $x<2$ so the right side is $x$. Then $2x=x$, $x=0$.
- If $x\ge\frac12$: the left side is $1$ (since $2x\ge1$ and $x+2>1$), so $\min(x,2)=1$, $x=1$.

Both check. **Answer: $x=0$ and $x=1$**

Suppose that $f(x)$ is a PUP of positive degree. Prove that if $f$ has more than one root, then it has infinitely many distinct roots.
answer: $f$ is nondecreasing, so it is $0$ on the whole interval between two roots.

solutions.title: Monotonicity
solutions.body:
In normal arithmetic,
$$f(x)=\min(nx+a_n,\,(n-1)x+a_{n-1},\,\dots,\,x+a_1,\,a_0),$$
a minimum of lines with nonnegative slopes. Each line is nondecreasing, so $f$ is nondecreasing: $x\le y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y)$.

If $r_1<r_2$ are roots, then for every $z\in[r_1,r_2]$, $0=f(r_1)\le f(z)\le f(r_2)=0$, so $f(z)=0$. That's infinitely many roots. ∎

A **root** of a PUP $f$ is a real $x$ with $f(x)=0$. The **parallel square root** $\sqrt[\circ]{a}$ is the unique solution of $x^{\odot2}=a$, and the **parallel reciprocal** $\hat a$ is the unique solution of $a\odot x=0$ (here $0$ is the identity $I$ with $I\odot x=x$).

Suppose $f(x)=(a\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(b\odot x)\oplus c$ is a quadratic PUP that has exactly one root. Find a formula for this root in terms of $a$, $b$, and $c$, using only the operations $\oplus$, $\odot$, parallel-universe exponentiation, parallel square roots, and parallel reciprocals.

solutions.title: Translate, then translate back
solutions.body:
In normal arithmetic $f(x)=\min(2x+a,\,x+b,\,c)$. For large $x$ (beyond $\max(\frac{c-a}2,c-b)$) $f(x)=c$, and $f(x)\le c$ always; $f$ is nondecreasing. So if $c<0$ there are no roots and if $c=0$ there are infinitely many; exactly one root forces $c>0$.

With $c>0$, $f(x)=0$ means $\min(2x+a,x+b)=0$ (it is below $c$). The function $\min(2x+a,x+b)$ is strictly increasing, and it is $0$ exactly when both $x\ge-\frac a2$ and $x\ge-b$ with equality in one, i.e.
$$x=\max\left(-\tfrac a2,-b\right)=-\min\left(\tfrac a2,b\right).$$
Translating back: $\frac a2=\sqrt[\circ]{a}$, $\min$ is $\oplus$, negation is the parallel reciprocal, so
$$x=\widehat{\left(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b\right)}.$$
Equivalent forms such as $\sqrt[\circ]{\widehat{a\oplus b^{\odot2}}}$ also work. (But $\sqrt[\circ]{\hat a}\oplus\hat b$ does not — it is $\min(-\frac a2,-b)$; reciprocals reverse $\oplus$.) ∎

solutions.title: Parallel-universe verification
solutions.body:
Let $x=\widehat{(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)}$. Using $\widehat{y^{\odot n}}=(\hat y)^{\odot n}$, a common "denominator" $(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)^{\odot 2}$, the distributive law (Problem 2) and Problem 4:
$$f(x)=\Big[a\oplus\big(b\odot\sqrt[\circ]{a}\big)\oplus b^{\odot2}\oplus(c\odot a)\oplus(c\odot b^{\odot2})\Big]\odot\widehat{(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)}^{\odot2}.$$
Since $c>0$, $a\oplus(c\odot a)=a$ and $b^{\odot2}\oplus(c\odot b^{\odot2})=b^{\odot2}$. By Problem 4c the bracket is $(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)^{\odot2}$, so $f(x)=(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)^{\odot2}\odot\widehat{(\sqrt[\circ]{a}\oplus b)^{\odot2}}=0$. ∎

solutions.title: Two cases

For a factorization $(k,r,s)$, since $r\le s$ we have $r\oplus s=r$, and by Problem 8, $g(x)=(a\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(a\odot r\odot x)\oplus c$ and $r+s=c-a$. In normal arithmetic, $f(x)=\min(2x+a,x+b,c)$ and $g(x)=\min(2x+a,x+a+r,c)$.

**Case 1: $2b<a+c$** (so $b-a<c-b$). Take $x=\frac{c-a}2$. Then $x<c-b$, so $f(x)=x+b<c$, while $2x+a=c$. So $g(x)\ne c$ forces $g(x)=x+a+r$, and $x+b=x+a+r$ gives $r=b-a$, $s=c-a-r=c-b$. Conversely $(a,b-a,c-b)$ works: then $a\odot r=b$ and $a\odot r\odot s=c$, so $g=f$ term by term.

**Case 2: $2b\ge a+c$** (so $c-b\le b-a$). Every $x$ satisfies $x\le b-a$ (so $2x+a\le x+b$) or $x\ge c-b$ (so $c\le x+b$); hence $f(x)=\min(2x+a,c)$. If $r<c-a-r$, pick $x$ strictly between; then $x+a+r<2x+a$ and $x+a+r<c$, so $g(x)=x+a+r$, which must equal $2x+a$ or $c$ — giving $x=r$ or $x=c-a-r$, a contradiction. So $r\ge\frac{c-a}2$; but $r\le s$ and $r+s=c-a$ give $r\le\frac{c-a}2$. So $r=s=d=\frac{c-a}2$, $k=a$. Conversely, by Problem 4b, $a\odot(x\oplus d)^{\odot2}=(a\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus(a\odot d^{\odot2})=(a\odot x^{\odot2})\oplus c=f(x)$.

In each case exactly one factorization exists. ∎
